I went down the same path starting about a decade ago with airplane mode, and deleting apps until my phone was so boring and rarely used I canceled my cell subscription about 8 years ago.

Have not carried a phone at all since. I rarely carry any electronics at all and exclusively use cash in person to make me mostly digitally invisible IRL.

Stopped using X and all big tech services. Google, Apple, Microsoft... even deleted my Facebook and Linkedin with thousands of connections. Github I have not used in years and will probably delete once I finish migrating repos to my self hosted git.

Other than email, Matrix, and online forums like this one, I pretty much just use a terminal, and will probably do those things in a terminal soon too as my locally hosted AI helps me rapidly write better CLI tooling.

Also exclusively use freely licensed open source software and self host almost everything I rely on, including AI. I have never been happier or more productive in my entire life.

I'm a fan of Marshall McLuhan, famous for "The Medium is the Message". When Twitter first arrived, I thought "what is the message delivered by a medium that limits thoughts to 140 characters at a time?". My take: "thoughts that are dirt-simple are the most welcome." Also, "what is the message delivered by a medium that freely interrupts me at any time?" (I never investigated the options to not be interrupted.) perhaps "There's no need to worry about having my own thought train interrupted .... "

Nothing I've heard or seen about Twitter is enticing.... but I'm old and cranky. Not quite as old and cranky as Donald Knuth, who stepped away from email after 15 years, writing:

I have been a happy man ever since January 1, 1990, when I no longer had an email address. I'd used email since about 1975, and it seems to me that 15 years of email is plenty for one lifetime.

Email is a wonderful thing for people whose role in life is to be on top of things. But not for me; my role is to be on the bottom of things. What I do takes long hours of studying and uninterruptible concentration. I try to learn certain areas of computer science exhaustively; then I try to digest that knowledge into a form that is accessible to people who don't have time for such study.

This is a great blog post. I do a lot of similar things on my phone (GrapheneOS, airplane mode, CoMaps).

The thing that I’d been looking for on this minimal setup was a way to prevent access to the browser or installing apps at will. It was easy enough when I was on iOS. I just used Apple Configurator [1] to block Safari and the App Store, but on GrapheneOS, there was no great option.

Recently I made a device owner app [2] which allows hiding any UI app and locking itself. It ended up being quite an elegant solution as it allows full access to app stores for updates (new apps you install are hidden until you unlock and approve them). The only way around it is with the lock code or a factory reset.

This makes my phone a quite private device whose functionality I intentionally set ahead of time. It can only do what the apps I’ve chosen can do. I prefer browsing and similar on a computer.

[1] Apple’s Mac MDM app anyone can use. You need a Mac and to factory reset your phone first.

[2] https://beeswax.getflourish.org/

Although he mentioned how easily cellular location data can be obtained from telecom operators, both legally and illegally, he forgot to mention that mercenary groups continuously obtain cellular location data through SS7/Diameter attacks in a continuous manner rather than using any special exploitation technique. We recently had a case involving tracking a few civilians in different foreign jurisdictions having our agency contracted a specialist company that provided us with cellular location data of the targets on a 24/7 basis. This can be used against any operator in any country, with only one of two pieces of PII required: the IMEI or the phone number (with the second piece always retrieved once the first is looked up).

For more details read https://citizenlab.ca/research/uncovering-global-telecom-exp...

There's another strong benefit to digital minimalism, which is the reduction in personal software footprint. The more software and network dependencies one is using, the greater security risks they take on. We live in an age where the supply chain risk is greater than ever, and it's useful to be mindful of the stacks our digital lives rest on. "How much can I get done with as little software and Internet dependencies as possible?" has always been an important question to be asking ourselves, and it's even truer now. Minimalism is not just a helpful principle to support our own cognitive wellness, but for our digital wellness as well.

> If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time. If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once.

That's precisely why something like signed distributions packages are way more secure than curl bash'ing.

But many simply don't understand that. We had plenty of forged Web certificates likely. And even without that, with curl bash'ing anything sensitive you have to cross fingers that the server ain't serving one in 10 000 request with a backdoored version.

With curl bash'ing everybody is trusting every single time that the server ain't compromised or intentionally malicious.

At this point I've lost any hope: people simply don't understand security.

And as long as we'll have people saying that curl bash'ing is just as safe as signed distros packages, we'll have daily posts about major security incidents.

Security is a mindset and most people simply don't have it.

minimalism, privacy, security, these are all mostly a pursuit of luxury.

ive spent a lot of time on that topic, and tech always comes up just short of producing a truly distinguishing luxury good.

the ones that succeeded became the macbook and iphone, blackberry, early facebook when it was only open to ivy schools, blue check twitter, tidal, early slack, Signal, and some others.

the looming question is, what is luxury? the answer as a positive definition is a kind of alchemical mystery. its failure mode is vulgarity, its imitations are cheap, economics only criticizes it, and its very context specific.

my working model is a triad of desirable, thoughtfulness, and belonging, where you can describe a luxury product on these axis and predict whether it will succeed.

for minimalism, notable challenges are things like the ReMarkable tablets that are high desire and thoughtfulness but lack the integration for belonging.

post-systemd Linux has low belonging vs the bsd communities, and is kind of mid in nerd desire and has too much slop attached to be thoughtful.

when you take an obvious luxury product like the proverbial LP pullover or a Ferrari, they imbue a belonging, where an entry level watch or a lamborghini do not. "class" was always a dumb framework bc its critical instead of constructive.

digital minimalist luxury hasn't really been invented yet in spite of some really good attempts. id argue because they lack something in this triad.
